title: Rama gone, Ravana gone
hook: raam gaio raavan gaio: Rama went, and Ravana with his large family went too (Salok M9 50, ang 1429)

segments.voice: Yesterday, jhooth, and your line: hold it lightly. Did you lean a little less on one thing you care about? Yesterday's salok said nothing stays, like a wall of sand. Today's names names. Day six hundred one.

Every autumn across north India, at Dussehra, crowds gather in open fields to watch giant effigies of Ravana, the ten-headed king of Lanka in the Ramayana, go up in flames. Children sit on their parents' shoulders. Fireworks crack inside the figure. And the story behind it, of Rama, the hero king, and his long war with Ravana to win back Sita, is one of the best-known stories in South Asia. Everyone in Guru Tegh Bahadur's world knew it. So when one of his saloks opens with those two names side by side, his listeners would have sat up. What could he possibly be saying about them?
screen: `DUSSEHRA: RAVANA IN FLAMES.` → `RAMA, THE HERO KING.` → `TWO NAMES SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: The fiftieth salok says raam gaio raavan gaio, jaa kau bahu parvaar. In paraphrase: Rama went, and Ravana went, who had such a large family. Says Nanak, nothing stays steady; the world is like a dream. Gaio means went, departed. Parvaar is family, the whole household. Ravana, in the epic, had a vast family and kingdom. And the salok's point is very simple: the greatest hero in the story, and the greatest villain, both left this world. The good king and the proud one, the one people worship and the one they burn. Death took both. Here it's worth saying who believes what. For many Hindus, Rama is God come to earth, deeply loved and worshipped. Sikh teaching speaks of God as never born and never dying, and Sikhs read this salok as being about Rama the king in the story, a man who walked the earth and left it. The salok isn't mocking anyone's faith. It's using the most famous names anyone knew to make the plainest point there is. And that's how it lands. If even they went, the hero with all his virtue, the villain with all his power and his huge family, then nobody's status, goodness or strength buys a longer stay. It's not meant to make us gloomy. It's meant to make us honest. Our own name, our own family, our own little kingdom, will go the same way. What lasts, as we've heard again and again in these saloks, is the Name of the Lord. Even they went. So, gently, will we.
screen: `GAIO: WENT, DEPARTED.` · `PARVAAR: A VAST FAMILY.` · `THE HERO AND THE PROUD ONE.` · `WHO BELIEVES WHAT ABOUT RAMA.` · then, large: `EVEN THEY WENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of the great who passed. Sit quietly and bring to mind three people who once seemed larger than life: a famous leader, a great artist, someone in your own family everyone looked up to. Picture each one at the height of their strength. Then remember that each has gone, or will. Let it be calm, not sad. Then turn to your own life with the same honesty: this, too, will pass. What would you like to fill it with? If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
Rama gone. The fiftieth salok says Rama went, and Ravana with his great family went too; nothing stays steady, and the world is like a dream.
Your line: even they went. Today, when you feel very important, or very small, remember the line, and spend the next hour on what lasts. Day six hundred one.

howItsDone: This salok is read near the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; Sikh teachers explain it as a reminder that even the greatest figures of the old stories departed, so no one's status lasts.

original.note: Gurmukhi: parvaar, family or household. The salok says even Ravana, with his great parvaar, departed.

trapdoor: what you thought: the salok is a comment on the Ramayana's characters.

what a scholar hears: in Gurbani raam usually names the all-pervading One, but paired here with Ravana it points to the king of the epic, and Sikh commentators read it that way.

notes: Paraphrase of salok 50 (raam gaio raavan gaio jaa kau bahu parvaar; kaho naanak thir kachh nahee supne jio sansaar): please confirm wording and Ang 1429.

The 'who believes what' passage on Rama (Hindu devotion to Rama as God incarnate; Sikh teaching of God as ajooni, never born) is meant to be fair to both; a Keeper, and ideally a Hindu reviewer, should check it.

Dussehra effigy burning described as a north Indian practice. Ravana is introduced as the king of Lanka rather than 'the demon king', since some communities in South Asia hold him in respect; the hero/villain framing follows the epic as most listeners know it.
